title: Macbeth: ambition, power, guilt and the supernatural
specPoints: AO1: themes and ideas; AO2: imagery and motifs

tips.title: Ambition in three shapes
tips.body: Desire, fear, emptiness: Stars, hide your fires; to be safely thus; signifying nothing.

tips.title: Motifs carry themes
tips.body: Blood, sleep, darkness, clothing. Trace one through the acts and you have a theme across the whole text.

tips.title: Guilt crosses
tips.body: He feels it at once and hardens; she denies it and breaks. A little water in Act 2; Out, damned spot in Act 5.

tips.title: The supernatural is ambiguous
tips.body: Banquo sees the witches too; only Macbeth sees the dagger and the ghost. Say what each reading gives you.

tips.title: Theme as a claim
tips.body: Not "ambition is a theme" but "ambition becomes fear once it is satisfied". A claim is conceptualised; a list is not.

why.matters: Most exam questions on *Macbeth* name a theme or an idea: ambition, power, guilt, the supernatural, appearance and reality. An answer that can turn the theme into a claim, and follow one of the play's own images across the acts to prove it, is doing exactly what the top level describes. The themes also connect, and seeing how ambition turns to fear, fear to tyranny, and tyranny to guilt gives every answer a way to move from a printed scene to the play as a whole.

examples.title: When winning becomes keeping
examples.body: People who reach the top of anything, a company, a sport, a government, often describe the same change Macbeth does: the effort that went into getting there turns into the fear of losing it. Stories of leaders who become more suspicious the longer they stay in power follow the shape of Act 3.

examples.title: A stain that will not wash
examples.body: Everyday speech still uses the play's images for guilt: having blood on your hands, a stain on your record, losing sleep over something you did. Shakespeare did not invent all of them, but *Macbeth* is where the image of guilt as a mark that will not wash off is given its most famous form.

steps.title: Ambition: from desire to fear
steps.body:
Ambition is the flaw Macbeth names in himself, and the play follows it through three shapes.

**Desire.** At first it is a wish he hides: “Stars, hide your fires” (Macbeth, 1.4); “Let not light see my black and deep desires”. In Act 1 Scene 7 he calls it “Vaulting ambition, which o’erleaps itself”, the only spur he has.

**Fear.** Once he has the crown, ambition turns into the need to keep it. “To be thus is nothing, But to be safely thus” (Macbeth, 3.1). He looks at the crown and sees “Upon my head they plac’d a fruitless crown”, because Banquo's sons will inherit it. Every later murder is done to make the first one safe.

**Emptiness.** At the end the thing he wanted means nothing: “I have liv’d long enough” (Macbeth, 5.3); life is “Life’s but a walking shadow”, “a tale Told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, Signifying nothing”.

Lady Macbeth's ambition runs beside his and ends sooner: in Act 3 she already knows that “Naught’s had, all’s spent”.

rows: Let not light see my black and deep desires
To be thus is nothing, but to be safely thus
props.title: Ambition in four lines

visuals.alt: A table of the four shapes ambition takes in Macbeth, each with a line: desire, flaw, fear and emptiness

check.prompt: What does To be thus is nothing, but to be safely thus show about Macbeth's ambition after the murder?
check.solution: Being king is nothing unless it is safe. The line comes just before he arranges Banquo's murder, and it shows ambition changing from wanting to keeping, which is why the killing does not stop.

markScheme.description: It has become fear: the crown is worthless to him unless he can keep it, so he must kill again

options: That he no longer believes the witches
That he is content now that he is king, and has decided to rule wisely and peacefully without any more killing, because he has everything the witches promised him
It has become fear: the crown is worthless to him unless he can keep it, so he must kill again
That he wants to give the crown back to Malcolm

steps.title: Power and kingship: the good king and the tyrant
steps.body:
The play sets two kinds of power side by side. Duncan's is care: he plants and makes things grow. Macbeth's is fear: he rules by killing.

**Nature responds to the murder of a king.** The night Duncan dies is unnatural. Ross says that by the clock it is day, and yet “dark night strangles the travelling lamp”. An old man reports that a falcon was killed by an owl, and that Duncan's horses broke loose; “they eat each other” (the Old Man, 2.4). For an audience that believed a king ruled by God's will, killing one broke the order of the world, and the play shows the world breaking.

**Tyranny.** Under Macbeth Scotland suffers: “Each new morn New widows howl, new orphans cry” (Macduff, 4.3). His lords obey without loyalty: “Those he commands move only in command, Nothing in love” (Angus, 5.2). His title seems to “Hang loose about him, like a giant’s robe Upon a dwarfish thief” (Angus, 5.2). The image of stolen clothes that do not fit runs through the play, from the borrowed robes of Cawdor to this.

**Restoration.** Malcolm names “the king-becoming graces”, and the play ends with him hailed king.

rows: A giant's robe on a thief
props.title: Two kings

visuals.alt: A table comparing Duncan and Macbeth as kings: how each rules, the image for each, and how their lords respond

check.prompt: Why does nature seem to go wrong on the night Duncan is murdered?
check.solution: Darkness at noon, an owl killing a falcon, horses turning wild and eating each other: the unnatural events mirror an unnatural act. The Doctor's line in Act 5, Unnatural deeds do breed unnatural troubles, states the idea directly.

markScheme.description: Killing a king was believed to break God's order, so the play shows the world disordered: darkness in the day, horses eating each other

options: Because Macbeth is frightened of the dark
Because there was a real storm in Scotland that night which Shakespeare read about in his history book, and he included it to make the play accurate to the chronicle
Because the witches cast a spell on the weather
Killing a king was believed to break God's order, so the play shows the world disordered: darkness in the day, horses eating each other

steps.title: Guilt: blood, sleep and hands
steps.body:
Guilt in *Macbeth* is shown through three images that return again and again: blood, sleep and hands.

**Blood.** Immediately after the murder: “Will all great Neptune’s ocean wash this blood” (Macbeth, 2.2); he answers himself that his hand would rather turn the green sea red. Lady Macbeth: “A little water clears us of this deed” (Lady Macbeth, 2.2). By Act 3 blood has become a law: “It will have blood, they say, blood will have blood” (Macbeth, 3.4). In Act 5 she smells it: “all the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand”.

**Sleep.** “Methought I heard a voice cry” (Macbeth, 2.2) Sleep no more; “Macbeth does murder sleep” (Macbeth, 2.2). He could not say Amen, which “Stuck in my throat”. The king who killed a sleeping man cannot sleep; his wife walks in hers.

**Hands.** After the murder she holds up her own: “My hands are of your color, but I shame To wear a heart so white” (Lady Macbeth, 2.2). In Act 5 she washes them for a quarter of an hour at a time, and cries “Out, damned spot” (Lady Macbeth, 5.1).

Guilt works differently on each. He sees it at once and then hardens; she denies it and then breaks.

rows: My hands are of your color
props.title: Three images of guilt

visuals.alt: A table of three images of guilt in Macbeth, blood, sleep and hands, with how each appears in Act 2 and in Act 5

check.prompt: How is guilt shown differently in Macbeth and in Lady Macbeth?
check.solution: In Act 2 he cannot stop talking about blood and sleep, and she says a little water will clear them. By Act 5 he has supp'd full with horrors and feels almost nothing, and she cannot stop washing her hands. The two lines of guilt cross, and the images show it.

markScheme.description: He feels it at once and then grows numb; she denies it at first and later breaks under it

options: He feels it at once and then grows numb; she denies it at first and later breaks under it
Neither of them feels guilt at any point
Only Macbeth feels guilt; Lady Macbeth never does
Both of them feel exactly the same guilt at exactly the same moments, which is why they both see Banquo's ghost at the banquet and both walk in their sleep in Act 5

steps.title: The supernatural: witches, a dagger, a ghost
steps.body:
Three kinds of supernatural event happen in the play, and each can be read in more than one way.

**The witches** are seen by Banquo as well as Macbeth, so they are real in the world of the play. They foretell; they do not command.

**The dagger.** Before the murder Macbeth sees “Is this a dagger which I see before me” (Macbeth, 2.1); he tries to take it and cannot. He calls it “A dagger of the mind, a false creation” (Macbeth, 2.1). Is it sent to lead him, or made by his own mind? The play gives him both explanations in one speech.

**The ghost.** At the banquet only Macbeth sees Banquo, and cries “Never shake Thy gory locks at me” (Macbeth, 3.4). His wife tells him it is the painting of his fear, like the air-drawn dagger. The lords see nothing.

**The apparitions** in Act 4 are shown by the witches and tell truths that mislead: “Beware Macduff; Beware the Thane of Fife”; “none of woman born Shall harm Macbeth”; “Great Birnam wood to high Dunsinane hill”.

The supernatural in *Macbeth* sits exactly on the line between the world and the mind, and that is where the play wants its audience to stand.

visuals.alt: A table of four supernatural events in Macbeth, who sees each, and what each could be

check.prompt: Why does it matter that only Macbeth sees the dagger and Banquo's ghost, while Banquo also sees the witches?
check.solution: Banquo's presence makes the witches external; Macbeth's solitude makes the dagger and the ghost ambiguous. He himself calls the dagger a dagger of the mind, a false creation, and his wife calls the ghost the painting of his fear. Shakespeare leaves the line between world and mind uncertain on purpose.

markScheme.description: The witches are real in the play's world, while the dagger and ghost could be his guilt, so both readings stay open

options: It shows that Banquo is blind
The witches are real in the play's world, while the dagger and ghost could be his guilt, so both readings stay open
It makes no difference to the play
It proves that Macbeth is mad from the very beginning of the play, and that the witches are also imaginary because Banquo is only pretending to see them in order to trick Macbeth into murder

steps.title: Tracing a motif: darkness
steps.body: A motif is an image that returns, and tracing one through the play is the quickest way to write about a theme across the whole text.

visuals.problem: Trace the motif of darkness through Macbeth and say what it shows.

steps.text: Act 1: Macbeth, “Stars, hide your fires”; Lady Macbeth, “Come, thick night”.
steps.note: Both call for darkness to hide what they want. Darkness is concealment, chosen.

steps.text: Act 2: Ross says “dark night strangles the travelling lamp” in the daytime after the murder.
steps.note: Now darkness has spread from them to the world: the day itself is dark.

steps.text: Act 3: Macbeth before Banquo's murder, “Come, seeling night”; “Light thickens”.
steps.note: He calls on night again, alone this time; seeling means sewing shut, as a falconer sews a hawk's eyes.

steps.text: Act 5: Lady Macbeth sleepwalks with a candle; she has light by her continually, the gentlewoman says.
steps.note: The woman who called for thick night is now afraid of the dark.

steps.text: The pattern: darkness called for, then spreading, then feared.
steps.note: The motif traces the theme of guilt: what was invited cannot be sent away.

visuals.alt: A flow chart of the motif of darkness in Macbeth: called for in Act 1, spreading to the day in Act 2, called on again in Act 3, and feared in Act 5

check.prompt: Why is Lady Macbeth's need for a light by her continually in Act 5 a strong point to make about the darkness motif?
check.solution: In Act 1 she invites darkness to hide the deed: Come, thick night. In Act 5 she cannot be without a light. The reversal is the motif doing the work of the theme, and naming both ends of it is a whole-text move.

markScheme.description: She called for thick night in Act 1 and now fears the dark, so the motif measures her fall

options: It shows that she is afraid of the witches
It shows that the castle at Dunsinane was very dark and poorly lit, and that she had difficulty seeing where she was going when she walked about at night in her nightgown
She called for thick night in Act 1 and now fears the dark, so the motif measures her fall
It shows that she has become religious

steps.title: Appearance and reality: fair is foul
steps.body:
The witches' first chant, “Fair is foul, and foul is fair” (the witches, 1.1), states a theme that runs through every relationship in the play: nothing is what it seems.

**Faces.** Duncan says “There’s no art To find the mind’s construction in the face” (Duncan, 1.4). Lady Macbeth tells her husband “look like the innocent flower, But be the serpent under’t”. Macbeth, persuaded, says “False face must hide what the false heart doth know” (Macbeth, 1.7).

**Smiles.** After the murder, Duncan's son Donalbain says “There’s daggers in men’s smiles” (Donalbain, 2.3), and flees.

**Words.** The witches' prophecies are true in their words and false in their meaning. Banquo warns of it in Act 1; Macbeth learns it in Act 5, when “Though Birnam wood be come to Dunsinane” and Macduff was “from his mother’s womb Untimely ripp’d”.

The theme makes the audience a judge. It sees the asides and the soliloquies, the gap between what characters say to each other and what they say alone, and so it knows what the characters on stage cannot.

rows: The place of the king's murder
props.title: Fair is foul

visuals.alt: A table of four pairs in Macbeth where what seems fair hides what is foul

check.prompt: How does the theme of appearance and reality make the audience a judge?
check.solution: Macbeth says Stars, hide your fires in an aside; Lady Macbeth plans aloud in soliloquy. The audience hears what Duncan cannot, and watches him trust. The gap between face and mind is the theme, and the audience stands inside it.

markScheme.description: Asides and soliloquies let the audience see the gap between what characters show and what they intend

options: The audience is asked to vote at the end of the play on whether Macbeth is guilty, which is why Malcolm addresses the final speech to the audience rather than to the thanes
The audience cannot tell what is real at any point
It does not; the characters always say what they mean
Asides and soliloquies let the audience see the gap between what characters show and what they intend

steps.title: Plan a theme answer on guilt
steps.body:
Take a question in the exam's shape: *Starting with Act 5 Scene 1, explore how Shakespeare presents guilt in Macbeth.* Plan it in five lines.

1. The idea: what guilt does to each of them, and how the play shows it.
2. Two methods in the sleepwalking scene: the prose, the repeated washing, the fragments of earlier scenes.
3. One echo from Act 2: a little water, or murdered sleep.
4. One contrast: Macbeth's guilt in Act 5, supp'd full with horrors.
5. One sentence of context tied to a line: guilt as sin, and the Doctor's more needs she the divine.

Then write the paragraph on the echo.

boxes.title: Idea
boxes.body: Guilt breaks her and numbs him

boxes.title: In the scene
boxes.body: Prose; washing; fragments of the past

visuals.alt: Four boxes planning an answer on guilt starting from the sleepwalking scene: idea, methods in the scene, echo, and context

check.prompt: Why is it significant that Lady Macbeth speaks in prose in the sleepwalking scene?
check.solution: She spoke in verse as a queen and a planner; asleep, she speaks in broken prose, in fragments of past scenes. The form is a method: the loss of verse is the loss of control. She is not speaking to the doctor at all; she does not know he is there.

markScheme.description: Her controlled verse has broken down, so the form of her speech shows the breakdown of her mind

options: Her controlled verse has broken down, so the form of her speech shows the breakdown of her mind
Because prose was used for royal characters
Because she is speaking to the doctor
Because Shakespeare ran out of time to write the scene in verse and left it in prose, which is why the scene is so short compared with the other scenes in the fifth act of the play

steps.title: Themes as an argument, not a list
steps.body:
A top-level answer on a theme has an idea about it, not a list of places where it appears. The Level 6 descriptor asks for a conceptualised response.

**Turn the theme into a claim.** Not *ambition is a theme in Macbeth* but *Shakespeare presents ambition as something that cannot stop: once it has what it wanted it becomes fear*.

**Use the motifs as evidence.** Blood, sleep, darkness and clothing are the play's own way of carrying its themes, and tracing one across the acts is a whole-text move.

**Connect themes.** Ambition leads to guilt; guilt drives tyranny; tyranny breaks nature; the supernatural stands on the line between guilt and fate. An answer that shows one theme feeding another is exploring ideas.

**Tie context to a line.** The divine right of kings explains why Ross's dark day matters; James I's interest in witchcraft explains why the witches frightened; neither replaces the line.

boxes.title: Supernatural
boxes.body: On the line between fate and mind

visuals.alt: Four boxes on how the themes of Macbeth feed each other: ambition, guilt, power and the supernatural

check.prompt: Which opening is conceptualised in the way the top level rewards, for a question on ambition?
check.solution: The opening about ambition turning to fear makes a claim that the rest of the essay can prove. The others list where the theme appears, announce a topic, or define a word. Only the claim is conceptualised.

markScheme.description: Shakespeare presents ambition as something that cannot stop: once it has the crown it turns to fear, and the fear kills more than the desire did

options: Ambition means wanting to succeed
Shakespeare presents ambition as something that cannot stop: once it has the crown it turns to fear, and the fear kills more than the desire did
Ambition is one of the main themes in Macbeth and it is shown in many places throughout the play, for example when Macbeth kills Duncan and when he kills Banquo and Macduff's family
In this essay I will write about ambition in Macbeth

steps.title: The themes in one page
steps.body:
Four themes, each with its images, each feeding the next.

- **Ambition:** desire (Stars, hide your fires), flaw (vaulting ambition), fear (to be safely thus), emptiness (signifying nothing).
- **Power:** Duncan's care and Macbeth's fear; nature broken by regicide; the giant's robe on a dwarfish thief; Malcolm's king-becoming graces.
- **Guilt:** blood, sleep, hands; he hardens, she breaks.
- **The supernatural:** witches seen by two; a dagger and a ghost seen by one; truths that deceive.
- **Appearance and reality:** fair is foul; the innocent flower and the serpent; daggers in men's smiles.
- **Motifs:** blood, sleep, darkness, clothing; trace one across the acts for the whole-text move.

visuals.alt: A summary table of four themes and the motif to trace for each

check.prompt: Which character says Unnatural deeds do breed unnatural troubles?
check.solution: The Doctor, after watching Lady Macbeth walk in her sleep. The line joins two themes: the unnatural act of regicide and the guilt that follows it.

markScheme.description: the Doctor

questions.prompt: Macbeth calls his only motive vaulting ambition. What image is behind the phrase?
questions.solution: Vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself, and falls on the other: the rider jumps too hard and comes down on the far side. The image predicts the fall inside the ambition.

markScheme.description: A rider who leaps into the saddle so hard that he falls over the other side

options: A soldier climbing the walls of a castle with a ladder during a siege, who reaches the top and captures the flag, as Macbeth did in the battle against Norway at the start of the play
A bird flying higher and higher
A king sitting on a throne
A rider who leaps into the saddle so hard that he falls over the other side

questions.prompt: Complete Macbeth's line: Will all great Neptune's ocean wash this ... clean from my hand?
questions.solution: Blood. Neptune is the Roman god of the sea, and the answer Macbeth gives himself is no: his hand would rather turn the green sea red. Guilt is shown as a stain nothing can wash away.

markScheme.description: blood

questions.prompt: What unnatural events are reported after Duncan's murder?
questions.solution: Ross and an old man report them in Act 2 Scene 4: dark night strangles the travelling lamp; a falcon was killed by a mousing owl; Duncan's horses broke out and ate each other. Nature is shown turned upside down.

markScheme.description: Darkness in the day, a falcon killed by an owl, and Duncan's horses eating each other

options: Darkness in the day, a falcon killed by an owl, and Duncan's horses eating each other
The sun rises twice
An earthquake that destroys Inverness, a flood that drowns the grooms, and a comet that appears over Scone on the day of the coronation, which the lords take as a sign against Macbeth
The witches appear in the courtyard

questions.prompt: What does Angus mean when he says Macbeth's title hangs loose about him, like a giant's robe upon a dwarfish thief?
questions.solution: A dwarf in a giant's stolen robe: the kingship is too big for him and not his. The clothing image runs from the borrowed robes of Cawdor in Act 1 to this.

markScheme.description: The crown is stolen and does not fit him: he is too small for the kingship he has taken

options: That Macbeth has grown thin from worry and his royal robes no longer fit him properly, so his servants have had to make him new ones for the battle against Malcolm's army
The crown is stolen and does not fit him: he is too small for the kingship he has taken
That Macbeth is a giant
That Macbeth has given his robes away

questions.prompt: Put these lines about blood and washing in the order the play presents them.
questions.solution: Act 2 Scene 2 twice, Macbeth then Lady Macbeth; Act 3 Scene 4; Act 5 Scene 1. Blood moves from a stain to a law to an obsession.

markScheme.description: the four lines in order

items: Will all great Neptune's ocean wash this blood
A little water clears us of this deed
It will have blood, they say, blood will have blood

questions.prompt: Macbeth calls the dagger he sees a dagger of the mind, a false creation. What does the phrase suggest?
questions.solution: He offers the explanation himself: the dagger may be a false creation, proceeding from the heat-oppressed brain. The play lets the supernatural and the psychological sit in one speech.

markScheme.description: It may come from his own guilty imagination rather than from any supernatural source

options: That he knows for certain the witches have sent the dagger to guide him to Duncan's chamber, and that he must follow it or the prophecy will not come true
That Lady Macbeth has put a real dagger in the air on a string
It may come from his own guilty imagination rather than from any supernatural source
That he has forgotten where he left his own dagger

questions.prompt: Which character says There's daggers in men's smiles, before fleeing to Ireland?
questions.solution: Donalbain, Duncan's younger son. The line sums up the theme of appearance and reality after the murder: nobody's face can be trusted.

markScheme.description: Donalbain

questions.prompt: What does seeling in Come, seeling night mean, and why is it a strong image?
questions.solution: Seeling was the falconer's practice of stitching a young hawk's eyelids shut. Macbeth asks night to do that to the pitiful eye of day before Banquo's murder, a violent image for darkness, and he says it alone.

markScheme.description: Sewing shut, as a falconer sewed a hawk's eyes to tame it: Macbeth asks night to blind the day

options: Selling, as in trading
Sealing, as a letter is sealed with wax and a stamp, because Macbeth is sending a secret letter to the murderers telling them where Banquo will be riding that evening
Ceiling, as in the roof of a room
Sewing shut, as a falconer sewed a hawk's eyes to tame it: Macbeth asks night to blind the day

questions.prompt: Why is Unnatural deeds do breed unnatural troubles a useful line for an answer connecting themes?
questions.solution: The Doctor speaks it after the sleepwalking scene. An unnatural deed, the murder of a king, breeds an unnatural trouble, a mind that cannot rest. The line connects power and guilt.

markScheme.description: It links the unnatural act of regicide to the guilt that follows, in one sentence

options: It links the unnatural act of regicide to the guilt that follows, in one sentence
Because Macbeth says it about himself
Because the Doctor says it about the weather, which proves that the storm on the night of the murder was sent by the witches as a punishment for Macbeth and his wife
Because it is the last line of the play

questions.prompt: How does Macbeth's ambition change after he becomes king?
questions.solution: To be thus is nothing, but to be safely thus. The fruitless crown and the barren sceptre show him that Banquo's line will inherit, and the killing continues to keep what he has.

markScheme.description: It becomes fear of losing the crown, which drives the murders of Banquo and Macduff's family

options: It disappears completely and he becomes a peaceful and generous king, until the witches appear again and tell him that he must kill Banquo to keep his throne, which he does against his will
It becomes fear of losing the crown, which drives the murders of Banquo and Macduff's family
It grows into a wish to become king of England too
It does not change

questions.prompt: Why is sleep such an important motif for guilt in the play?
questions.solution: Macbeth does murder sleep, the voice cries, and Glamis hath murder'd sleep. The crime and its punishment share an image: he who killed a sleeping man cannot sleep; his wife walks in hers.

markScheme.description: Macbeth killed a sleeping king, and the punishment is that he and his wife lose sleep

options: Because Duncan dies in his sleep of old age
Because the play is set entirely at night
Macbeth killed a sleeping king, and the punishment is that he and his wife lose sleep
Because Macbeth is tired from the battle at the start of the play and needs rest, and the witches keep him awake at night with their chanting on the heath, which is why he makes mistakes

questions.prompt: Which Roman god of the sea does Macbeth name in his line about washing the blood off his hand?
questions.solution: Neptune: Will all great Neptune's ocean wash this blood clean from my hand? The hyperbole measures the guilt: all the oceans would not be enough.

markScheme.description: Neptune

questions.prompt: What does the play's ending suggest about power?
questions.solution: Macduff enters with the usurper's cursed head; Malcolm is hailed King of Scotland and promises to reward the thanes. The ending restores order. Some productions hint that the cycle may continue, but the text itself ends with restoration.

markScheme.description: Order returns with a rightful king: Malcolm is hailed, and the tyrant's head is shown

options: That power always corrupts, because Malcolm immediately becomes a tyrant himself and orders the execution of Macduff for killing Macbeth without a trial, which starts the cycle again
That Scotland will be ruled by England from now on
That the witches will choose the next king
Order returns with a rightful king: Malcolm is hailed, and the tyrant's head is shown

questions.prompt: Put these moments in the darkness motif in the order the play presents them.
questions.solution: Act 1 Scene 4, Act 2 Scene 4, Act 3 Scene 2, Act 5 Scene 1. Darkness is called for, spreads to the day, is called on again, and at last is feared.

markScheme.description: the four moments in order

items: Dark night strangles the travelling lamp
She has light by her continually

questions.prompt: Starting with Act 5 Scene 1, explore how Shakespeare presents guilt in Macbeth. Write the opening idea and two paragraphs: one on the sleepwalking scene, and one on guilt elsewhere in the play.
questions.solution: Shakespeare presents guilt as the thing that returns to the place it was denied: Lady Macbeth told her husband that water would clean them, and guilt comes back to her hands. In the sleepwalking scene she speaks in prose, broken into fragments of the past, so that the form of her speech is the collapse of her control. “Out, damned spot” is a command to a stain that will not obey, and “who would have thought the old man to have had so much blood in him” replays the night of the murder as if she were still in it. Her most telling line is “all the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand”: the hyperbole of all the perfumes of the East measured against one little hand. The Doctor's judgement, “More needs she the divine than the physician”, frames her illness as sin rather than sickness, as a Jacobean audience would have understood it. Across the play the scene is an echo. After the murder she said “A little water clears us of this deed”, while Macbeth asked “Will all great Neptune’s ocean wash this blood” and could not sleep: “Macbeth does murder sleep”. In Act 2 he had the guilt and she the confidence; in Act 5 he has “I have supp’d full with horrors” and she cannot stop washing. Guilt in the play does not fall on the guilty equally or at once, but it arrives, and it arrives in the images they used to deny it.

Her most telling line is “all the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand”: the hyperbole of all the perfumes of the East measured against one little hand. The Doctor's judgement, “More needs she the divine than the physician”, frames her illness as sin rather than sickness, as a Jacobean audience would have understood it. Across the play the scene is an echo. After the murder she said “A little water clears us of this deed”, while Macbeth asked “Will all great Neptune’s ocean wash this blood” and could not sleep: “Macbeth does murder sleep”. In Act 2 he had the guilt and she the confidence; in Act 5 he has “I have supp’d full with horrors” and she cannot stop washing. questions.prompt: Write one analytical paragraph on how Shakespeare presents ambition changing over the play. Use at least three quotations from different acts.
questions.solution: Shakespeare presents ambition as something that cannot stop once it has begun, because what it wins it must then keep. In Act 1 it is a desire hidden from the light, “Stars, hide your fires”, and Macbeth knows it for what it is: “Vaulting ambition, which o’erleaps itself”, a rider leaping so hard he falls on the other side. The image predicts the fall inside the wish. In Act 3 the same ambition has become fear. “To be thus is nothing, But to be safely thus”, he says, and the word *safely* shows that the crown is now worth nothing in itself; it is worth only what it would cost to lose. The murders of Banquo and of Macduff's family follow from that fear, not from desire. By Act 5 ambition has emptied itself: the man who wanted everything says “I have liv’d long enough” and calls life “a tale Told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, Signifying nothing”. The structure makes the argument: desire in Act 1, fear in Act 3, emptiness in Act 5, so that the play shows ambition not as a wish for power but as a hunger that turns into terror and ends in nothing.

questions.prompt: A student writes: "The supernatural is just there to make the play scary." What is the better account?
questions.solution: The supernatural is frightening, and it also carries the play's central question: is Macbeth driven, or does he choose? Only he sees the dagger and the ghost; Banquo sees the witches too. The ambiguity is the point.

markScheme.description: It stands on the line between fate and mind: the dagger and ghost could be guilt, and the witches foretell but never command

options: It stands on the line between fate and mind: the dagger and ghost could be guilt, and the witches foretell but never command

The student is right: Shakespeare included the witches, the dagger and the ghost only to entertain an audience who enjoyed frightening scenes, and they have no connection to the play's themes or ideas

questions.prompt: Which answer ties context to a line in the way the top level rewards?
questions.solution: The answer about Ross's dark night connects a belief to a line and explains what the line does. The answer on the divine right gives the belief without a line; the others give facts with no link. The top level asks for exploration of context shown by specific, detailed links between context, text and task.

examTechnique.body:
**Name the theme as a claim.** A question on guilt or ambition wants an idea about it, and the Level 6 word is conceptualised.

**Use motifs for the whole-text move.** Blood from Act 2 to Act 5; darkness from Stars, hide your fires to a light by her continually; clothing from borrowed robes to a giant's robe on a thief.

**Connect themes.** Ambition feeds fear, fear feeds tyranny, tyranny breaks nature, and guilt follows.

**Context tied to a line.** The divine right of kings explains Ross's dark day; James I's interest in witchcraft explains the witches' power to frighten.
examinerErrors: Listing places where a theme appears without a claim about it.
Writing a paragraph on the divine right of kings with no line from the play.
Treating the supernatural as decoration rather than as part of the question of choice.
Misattributing lines: Donalbain says there are daggers in men's smiles; Ross reports that Duncan's horses broke loose, and the Old Man adds that they ate each other.
Ignoring the change in ambition after the murder.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer on a theme states a claim in its first sentence and proves it across the play. It traces a motif, blood or sleep or darkness, from one act to another, analyses the language at each point, and shows how one theme feeds another. Context appears as a belief that explains a line. The supernatural is treated as a question the play leaves open, and the answer says what each reading makes of the scene in front of it.
